assessment.nobel_worthiness: The nominal-rigidity and New Keynesian framework, with time-dependent price setting and interest-rate rules, underlies modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice. The scientific contribution is foundational and has had very large practical impact.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across many contributors. Calvo (staggered pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule) and Woodford (the microfounded synthesis and normative analysis) are the clearest core. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have strong claims on the empirical and DSGE side, and the three-person cap forces exclusions.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The key work dates from 1979 to 2003 and has been tested through several decades of policy use, including the post-2020 inflation episode.
uncertainties: Which subset best captures the core idea, given the 3-laureate cap
Ongoing debate over how well the framework performed in the post-2020 inflation and in heterogeneous-agent extensions
Common knowledge of the contributions rather than independent verification

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm trade framework changed how the gains from trade are analysed. It shifted attention from sectors to firm selection and reallocation and set the empirical agenda for firm-level trade research.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman's work on firm-level trade and on the organisation of production is closely related, and he is also credited under other candidates. Redding's quantitative extensions are important but later and more derivative.
assessment.maturity: Mature. More than two decades of intensive empirical use and extension. Krugman's 2008 prize covered the earlier new trade theory, so this is a distinct, later advance.
uncertainties: Overlap with Krugman's earlier prize and with the quantitative trade candidate
Whether Helpman's contribution is best credited here or through the political-economy of trade line

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Skill-biased and task-based accounts of technology and the quasi-experimental evidence on import competition link labour, trade and technology to wage inequality. The work is empirically credible and shaped both academic and policy debates on labour-market adjustment.
assessment.attribution: Autor has the central role across both the tasks framework and the China shock. Hanson (with Dorn and Autor) is central to the trade-shock evidence. Katz is central to the skill-premium and task literature. Dorn is a close contributor but more junior. The task framework also draws on contributors not on this list, such as Levy and Murnane.
assessment.maturity: Largely mature. The skill-premium work spans decades and the China-shock work is over ten years old with extensive replication and debate, though long-run welfare conclusions are still evolving.
uncertainties: Exclusion of Dorn and of non-listed task-framework contributors
Debate over the persistence and magnitude of the China shock and over the task-model interpretation
Overlap with the 2023 prize for Goldin on labour-market history

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law and finance programme made legal institutions and investor protection a core empirical object in finance and development. It opened a large research agenda on institutions and financial development.
assessment.attribution: The LLSV core of La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes and Shleifer is well defined. Vishny is an equally important co-author of the corporate-governance and market-inefficiency work but would be the fourth name.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The key papers date from the late 1990s and have been heavily cited and extended.
uncertainties: Substantial critique of the legal-origins hypothesis, its measurement and its causal interpretation
Whether the committee would credit the descriptive and conceptual contribution as sufficient
Considerations beyond scientific merit concerning individual candidates, which the criteria exclude from assessment

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel GMM estimators, such as Arellano-Bond and Blundell-Bond, are among the most widely used estimators in applied economics. They made credible estimation of dynamic relationships with unobserved heterogeneity routine across micro and macro fields.
assessment.attribution: The estimator papers by Arellano and Bond (1991) and Blundell and Bond (1998) carry clear and well-documented credit. Arellano's broader panel-data contributions strengthen the case. Blundell is also credited elsewhere on the list. Credit builds on earlier work (Anderson-Hsiao, Holtz-Eakin et al., Hansen's GMM).
assessment.maturity: Mature. More than 25 years of use. Known practical issues, such as instrument proliferation and weak instruments, are well understood.
uncertainties: Whether a widely used estimator is judged a sufficiently fundamental advance compared with conceptual discoveries
Priority claims of earlier GMM and panel-data contributors

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework quantifies how frictions in resource allocation across firms explain cross-country differences in productivity and income. It links micro data to aggregate development accounting, with real consequences for policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the central paper. Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) is a parallel founding contribution, and Rogerson is not on this credited list.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature, at about 15 to 17 years. It is widely adopted, but measurement challenges are still debated.
uncertainties: Sensitivity of measured misallocation to measurement error and to the model's assumptions about markups and adjustment costs
Omission of Richard Rogerson, who is not credited under this candidate
Whether the contribution is a refinement of the growth-accounting tradition or a sufficiently distinct discovery

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run series on top incomes and wealth, built from tax records and national accounts, transformed the empirical study of distribution. They created new public data resources and reopened a central question in the discipline, in line with the value of archival data work that also provides explanatory insight.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez (with Atkinson, who is deceased) pioneered the top-income series. Zucman is central to the wealth and offshore-wealth estimates. The data-building credit is clear, but the explanatory framework is less settled.
assessment.maturity: Mixed. The top-income series are about 20 years old and widely used, while the wealth and offshore estimates and the theoretical claims on r>g are more recent and contested.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over the wealth estimates, the treatment of taxes and transfers, and the explanatory framework
Zucman's relatively early career stage
Attribution to the late Anthony Atkinson and other contributors, who cannot be named under the credited names

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work tests full-insurance and informal risk-sharing models with household data and examines how village institutions, credit and information frictions shape insurance and investment. It supplied core empirical methods for development economics.
assessment.attribution: Townsend (risk-sharing tests and Thai data), Rosenzweig (household and marriage-market risk-sharing and human-capital work) and Udry (Ghana and Burkina Faso field evidence on risk, credit and investment) each have distinct, identifiable roles. Others, such as Deaton and Morduch, also contributed substantially.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The key work spans roughly 1990 to 2010, with established replication and continued development.
uncertainties: Full insurance is repeatedly rejected, so the contribution is better characterised as a framework plus a stylised fact than as a settled answer
Relationship to the 2015 and 2019 prizes, which already recognised development and micro-evidence contributions
Credit split among the three and omitted contributors
